checkpoints: Uniform interface means verb = operation and URL = resource noun (`POST /users` creates, `GET /users/:id` reads, `PUT` replaces the whole representation, `PATCH` updates part, `DELETE` removes) — a contract clients, proxies, and tooling rely on without knowing server internals.
Collapsing everything into POST loses the read/write distinction for caching proxies, so read cacheability disappears.
Collapsing everything into POST loses the idempotency signal that makes retries safe on flaky networks.
Collapsing everything into POST loses generic tooling such as gateways and client generators that understand the API without bespoke docs per action-URL.
Collapsing everything into POST loses meaningful status codes, since created and missing both degrade to a plain 200.
REST semantics are not arbitrary URL-naming convention — they encode the outcome contract in a standard, machine-visible way.
Client data is untrusted until it is checked, so it must be stopped right at the boundary, before it ever touches business logic.
Scattering ifs across the service means every handler invents its own rules, making coverage inconsistent and easy to miss.
Once a case is missed, the bad data travels deep into the system and only blows up at the DB layer — the point furthest from the root cause and hardest to trace.

The fix is putting all of that checking into ONE global validation layer at the boundary (a validation pipe, Bean Validation with `@Valid`, model binding + data annotations, or struct tags + a validator library), turning it into the single control point.
An invalid payload is rejected immediately with a 400 plus a structured error list — fail-fast.
Every route shares the same set of rules — consistency.
The service only ever receives clean, already-typed data — simplicity.

The input contract must be explicitly DECLARED as a clear schema, such as an annotated DTO/model or a tagged struct, rather than an implied set of ifs scattered everywhere, so it can be audited in one single place.

Hand-assembling the response envelope inside each handler duplicates the contract once per handler, so every new handler is another chance for the success and error shapes to drift apart — which has already happened here: one handler's success body includes `timestamp` while the other's doesn't, and one names the payload `data` while the other calls it `result`.

Returning `res.status(200)` from inside a catch block hides a real failure behind a success status code, so both the client and any monitoring or alerting keyed on HTTP status read a thrown error as if the request succeeded.

Collapsing every caught error into one hard-coded status (such as 500) erases the distinction between an expected domain error — like a referenced resource not being found — and a genuine server fault, so a case that should surface as 404 instead reads as an indistinguishable internal failure.

Forwarding a caught exception's raw `.message` straight into the JSON response body leaks internal implementation detail (driver, ORM, or other low-level error text) to external clients instead of returning a controlled, generic message.

The fix is not to patch each handler's shaping logic but to remove response construction from handlers entirely: a handler should return plain business data on success or throw a semantic domain exception (e.g. `NotFoundException`, `BadRequestException`) on failure, and do nothing else.

Success-response shaping belongs in exactly one place — a single global interceptor — so that every route in the API shares one canonical envelope shape instead of each handler re-implementing it slightly differently.

Error normalization belongs in exactly one place — a single global exception filter — which can branch on known versus unknown exception types, attach fields like details/timestamp/path, and fall back to a generic message for anything not explicitly recognized, so leaking internal detail becomes structurally impossible rather than a per-handler discipline.

Verifying this kind of centralization calls for contract-level tests rather than manual inspection: asserting every route's success response shares the same root keys, that a thrown domain not-found exception produces a 404 in the standard error envelope, and that an unrecognized error degrades to a generic 500 envelope whose message contains none of the original internal error text.

Applying pagination by slicing an already-fetched array in application memory after an unbounded `find()`/`SELECT *` still returns correct page contents for every request — the output looking right is exactly why this bug survives code review even though the entire table is read every time.

When a repository call carries no where/skip/take criteria, the data source returns every row in the table before any slicing happens; the cost is O(total rows) for I/O, ORM hydration, and JSON serialization on each request, independent of the requested page size — page 1 with limit 10 against 2 rows or 2,000,000 rows does the identical 'fetch everything' work.

Because this per-request cost scales with table size, p95 latency and memory climb roughly linearly as the table grows, and N concurrent requests each hold their own full in-memory copy of the table at once, multiplying the cost under load.

The fix is to push `page`/`limit` down into the query itself — `repo.find({ skip: (page - 1) * limit, take: limit })` or a query builder's `.skip().take()` — which compiles to a SQL `OFFSET`/`LIMIT` clause so the database performs the windowing and only one page of rows ever leaves the DB, crosses the network, or gets serialized.

Pushing pagination into the query changes only what happens between the repository call and the database — the controller's response shape and the contract given to the client stay identical, so the optimization is invisible to callers.

Computing `skip: (page - 1) * limit` as safe arithmetic depends entirely on the query DTO's `@Type(() => Number)`, `@IsInt`, `@Min(1)`, and default values already guaranteeing that `page`/`limit` are real, bounded, positive integers by the time they reach the service.

If raw, unvalidated query-string values fed that same offset formula instead, a non-numeric `page` would produce `NaN`, and a zero or negative `page` would produce a negative offset — which several databases either reject or silently treat as 'no offset,' leaking rows or erroring deep in the DB layer instead of failing cleanly with a 400 at the boundary.

Verifying the fix means diffing the returned rows for the same page/limit combinations before and after the change (contents must be identical), then confirming the win through query logging showing a single `SELECT ... LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2` instead of an unbounded `SELECT *`, or through load testing showing latency flatten instead of scale with table size, while re-confirming the boundary still rejects an invalid `page` with 400.

Offset-based pagination itself degrades at very deep pages because the database still has to walk past every skipped row before returning results; keyset/cursor pagination — filtering by `WHERE id > lastSeenId ORDER BY id LIMIT n` — avoids that cost by never asking the database to scan past rows it isn't returning.

Calling `SwaggerModule.createDocument(app, config)` inside a request handler means the full controller/DTO metadata scan and OpenAPI document assembly reruns on every single hit to that route, which is why an idle service shows rising CPU the moment something polls the endpoint repeatedly.

The generated OpenAPI document is a deterministic function of the code currently deployed in the running process — two requests handled by the same process, with no code change between them, can never produce a different document, so recomputing it per request just recreates a byte-identical artifact N times.

Because the expensive scan-and-assemble step yields the same output for the lifetime of a process, that work belongs at startup (or memoized on the first hit) rather than inside the request path; after that, serving the spec is nothing more than returning an already-built object.

The fix is to call `createDocument` exactly once during bootstrap, hold the resulting document, and have the route return that held object instead of rebuilding it — moving one function call out of the request handler removes the entire per-request scan.

Using `SwaggerModule.setup("swagger", app, document)` instead of hand-wiring the JSON route lets one generated document back both the human-readable UI at `/swagger` and the raw JSON at `/swagger-json`, so there is one artifact serving multiple surfaces rather than duplicated generation logic.

The document only changes when the code changes, and a code change requires a new build and a fresh process that runs bootstrap again — so generating the spec at startup is exactly as fresh as generating it per request, just at a fraction of the cost, which is the direct answer to "but what if the spec needs to change?"

There is no runtime scenario where a live, already-booted process needs to serve a newer spec than the one produced when it started, since nothing about its own routes or DTOs can mutate without a redeploy.

Correctness of the fix is verified by checking that the `/swagger-json` response body is byte-identical before and after the change, that latency and CPU flatten to the cost of serving a cached object even under continuous polling, and that after an actual code change plus redeploy the served document reflects the new schema — proving the switch to startup generation never sacrificed freshness.

The fixed root frame is { statusCode, error, message, details?, timestamp, path }: statusCode is a number for the client to branch on, and error is a machine-stable class name that never changes with display language, giving programmatic clients something to switch on that plain text cannot.

message is always ONE string for humans — a summary of the first error or a count — no matter how many field errors validation produces, while the full structured list lives in details, keeping message's type stable while still being machine-readable through details.

timestamp + path are the tracing metadata for when and where the error happened, and later join with logs/traces so production debugging can locate the exact request instead of just seeing a generic message.

Under the fixed root, details is typed per error class: validation returns an array of per-field errors each carrying a full path down to nested fields like `address.zip`, not-found returns { resource, id }, and an unexpected error omits details entirely — a conditional presence, never an explicit null/undefined.

The leak policy lives at the structural level: the catch-all boundary is the ONLY border between internals and the client, so known domain errors pass through with their own safe status + message while anything unrecognized automatically degrades to 500 with a generic message.
Stack traces, internal messages, and PII are logged server-side only, with no other path out, because handlers have no shortcut to respond directly.

Enforcement has to sit at one single global boundary — an exception filter, controller advice, exception middleware, or recover middleware depending on the stack — so handlers only throw meaningful domain exceptions with no way to "forget" and slip outside the contract, since per-handler discipline is the failure point, not a trustworthy design.

Structured details let the client react precisely — for example highlighting the exact wrong field — instead of showing only a generic message, which is the practical payoff of keeping message and details separate.

Full endpoint/status-code set: POST /projects returns 201 with the created representation (any new resource earns 201, not 200); GET /projects (list) returns 200; GET /projects/:id returns 200, or 404 if the id doesn't exist; PUT /projects/:id and PATCH /projects/:id both return 200 for a successful update; DELETE /projects/:id returns 204 with no body — every outcome gets a code chosen for what actually happened.
PUT and PATCH are not interchangeable: PUT is full-replace and requires the client to send every field (omitting one means clearing it), while PATCH updates only the fields actually sent.
The request DTO (e.g. CreateProjectDto) carries per-field metadata (type, example, required) via a decorator/annotation/attribute that the document builder scans into components.schemas.

The DTO is deliberately not the same shape as the stored record: the wire contract (what a client sends) and the internal persisted shape (which may gain fields, denormalize, or rename) are allowed to diverge because nothing external depends on storage shape, only on the DTO.

The security scheme is declared once at the document level and then attached per endpoint, and that attachment must mirror the real guard on that route — a mismatch in either direction (documented-protected-but-unguarded, or guarded-but-spec-shows-open) is a contract lie.

The pipeline: metadata lives beside the code; a document builder scans it at bootstrap (or build time for compiled-annotation stacks) into ONE generated document that feeds the human-readable docs UI, the raw JSON endpoint, frontend codegen/SDK generation, and a CI contract-test step.

The document must be generated rather than hand-authored, because hand-authoring reintroduces a second copy detached from the code that silently drifts the moment a DTO changes and the docs aren't updated.

Drift can still creep in even with generation because the spec metadata and the runtime validator are two separate declarations on the same field — a validator can be added without annotating the field for the spec (enforced but invisible to generated clients), or the two can disagree on a constraint; the countermeasure is preferring a single-source plugin/inference path, reviewing the pair together on every DTO change, and having CI contract-test the generated spec against real endpoint behavior.
States create (POST /users) returns 201 Created with the created representation, including the server-assigned id.
States a successful delete returns 204 No Content with an empty response body.
States reading a missing id returns 404 Not Found.
States the principle that the status code (the NUMBER) is what the client reads to learn success/failure, while the actual data or message lives in the body.
Names the concrete frontend pain from the prompt: a '200 for everything' API forces the client to parse the body against a bespoke convention just to find out whether the request succeeded.
Names at least one concrete downstream cost beyond frontend parsing — e.g. hidden failures from monitoring/proxies, or broken generic tooling (caching/retries/alerting) that depends on status codes.

States the fix: set the status per handler using the stack's idiom (a status decorator/ResponseEntity/CreatedAtAction-NoContent-NotFound/WriteHeader), translating a 'not found' domain result into the framework's real 404 exception instead of stuffing it inside a 200 body.
Names the core diagnosis: a hand-written doc (README + Postman collection) is a second copy of the contract that lives apart from the code, and nothing forces it to change when the code changes.

Directly answers 'why structural': a developer can rename a field, ship it, and the docs stay silently wrong until a client integrates against the old shape — no single mistake, the process has no enforcement point.
States the fix in one sentence: generate the spec FROM the code so drift becomes structurally impossible, rather than relying on discipline to keep two copies in sync.

Describes the generation mechanism: schema/operation metadata sits right next to the DTO/handler it describes (annotations/decorators scanned by a tool such as springdoc/Swashbuckle/swaggo), scanned into one OpenAPI document at bootstrap.
Names the concrete payoff: renaming a field changes the spec in the very same commit — there is no second file to forget, and the change is visible in the diff.

Names at least one concrete downstream consumer of the generated spec beyond human reading — e.g. frontend client SDK/type codegen, a mock server for parallel work, CI contract tests, or gateway request validation.
Notes the same document also drives the human-facing Swagger UI — one artifact, many surfaces, never a duplicate.
Answers 'how this catches the rename before integration': the frontend reviews a diff of the generated spec in the pull request and regenerates its types from it, with no verbal handoff required.
Idempotency is a statement about the final stored state, not about the response — calling an operation once or many times must converge to the same state.
GET only reads, so repeating it changes nothing.
PUT carries full-replace semantics — sending the same body again always overwrites to the same state.
DELETE ends at 'the resource is absent' — calling it again still ends there.
GET, PUT, and DELETE are all safe to blindly retry after a timeout, precisely because the client cannot tell whether the first attempt already landed.
POST creates a new resource each time, so a blind retry after a timeout risks creating a duplicate.

A second DELETE returning 404 while the first returned 204 does not break idempotency — idempotency only promises the state (resource gone) doesn't change on repeat, not that the response is identical; returning 204 again is a valid policy choice, but 404 is equally correct.

When the business needs reliable creation over an unreliable network, the client attaches an idempotency key to the POST (or the server keeps its own de-duplication record) so a retried request is recognized as the same logical create and isn't applied a second time.
